stances.claim: To answer why Napoles was freed of 16 alleged Sec 3-e RA 3019 violations, CJ read the 223-page Sandiganbayan decision People v. Revilla (May 22, 2023) penned by Justice Geraldine Faith A. Econg - NOT by Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang as erroneously reported by the Inquirer on May 23 and 'sadly repeated' in its May 26 editorial.

Understanding requires a backgrounder on plunder (RA 7080, July 12, 1991) vs graft (RA 3019, Aug 17, 1960) vs Revised Penal Code crimes (effective 'believe it or not' Jan 1, 1932); plunder is a relatively new crime.

Per Jinggoy Estrada v. Sandiganbayan (Feb 26, 2002), the anti-plunder law was 'crafted to avoid the mischief and folly of filing multiple informations' in the aftermath of the Marcos regime, where 'multitude and magnitude' of acts produced a 'legal nightmare' - the law helped unclog dockets while aggregating predicate acts (malversation, bribery, RA 3019 violations) into a single plunder charge punishable by reclusion perpetua to death.

Here, the OBM prosecutors charged Napoles separately with 16 RA 3019 violations AND filed a separate plunder charge against Revilla et al. (including Napoles) using THESE VERY SAME violations as predicates. Since Revilla et al. were earlier acquitted of plunder for failure to prove the predicate crimes, Napoles could no longer be found guilty of the same unproven predicate acts.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-collateral-effect mapping (same-predicates analysis as analytical core)

stances.claim: Justice Econg's 'masterpiece' patiently narrated trial testimonies, especially of Benhur Luy, identical to those in the plunder case - and she could have shortened her decision by simply referring to and not reproducing them.

CJ concurs with the Sandiganbayan - though Napoles remains detained on other pending cases. Regardless of agreement with the Revilla acquittal, CJ is 'bound by such judgment.' The prosecutors committed the 'legal nightmare' of multiple prosecutions the anti-plunder law sought to avoid - 'lucky Justice Econg did not chastise them for committing this legal blunder.'
stances.rhetorical_move: concurrence plus bound-by-judgment posture plus prosecution-blunder critique

stances.claim: Tribute: Division chairman Justice Efren N. de la Cruz - reliable, credible, honest, competent, and IMHO 'should have been promoted to the Supreme Court long ago.' But de la Cruz reaches compulsory retirement next year while the next SC vacancy is in June 2025; three former Sandiganbayan colleagues (Leonardo-de Castro, Peralta, Gesmundo) were promoted and all became CJs - and de la Cruz preceded CJ Gesmundo in the Sandiganbayan.

notable_anecdotes: CJ's explicit Inquirer correction - 'not by Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang as erroneously reported by the Inquirer on May 23 and sadly repeated in its editorial on May 26' - a rare instance of a regular columnist openly correcting his own publisher's reporting AND editorial in the same parenthetical.
The 'believe it or not, Jan. 1, 1932' aside about the Revised Penal Code's effectivity - a CJ signature didactic flourish.

The Jinggoy Estrada v. Sandiganbayan (February 26, 2002) verbatim quotation tracing the anti-plunder law's origin to Marcos-era 'multitude and magnitude' of acts and the 'legal nightmare' of multiple Informations - preserved as the canonical legislative-history explanation.

The doctrinal architecture: same predicate acts used in plunder cannot ground separate convictions if the plunder was acquitted for failure to prove those predicates - one of CJ's cleanest single-paragraph articulations of the anti-multiple-prosecution rationale.
The 'OBM prosecutors are lucky Justice Econg did not chastise them' line - gentle judicial-style finger-wagging.

The Justice Efren N. de la Cruz missed-promotion tribute - paired with the institutional arithmetic that THREE Sandiganbayan colleagues (Leonardo-de Castro, Peralta, Gesmundo) became CJ while de la Cruz himself was overlooked, with the specific note that de la Cruz preceded Gesmundo in the SBN. One of CJ's most poignant judicial-promotion laments.
The 'Justice Econg's masterpiece' compliment paired with the constructive editorial suggestion - showing CJ comfortable praising and critiquing the same judicial work in adjacent sentences.
Benhur Luy named as the central whistleblower-witness whose plunder-case testimony was 'identical to' the graft-case testimony - the link that made the second prosecution doctrinally improper.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban answers the public question why Janet Lim-Napoles (and several others) were freed of criminal responsibility for her alleged 16 separate Section 3-e violations of the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act (RA 3019) in the pork-barrel scam exposed by the Inquirer in 2013. He read the 223-page Sandiganbayan decision People v. Revilla (May 22, 2023) penned by Justice Geraldine Faith A. Econg - NOT by Presiding Justice Amparo Cabotaje-Tang as erroneously reported by the Inquirer on May 23 and sadly repeated in its May 26 editorial - with Justices Efren N. de la Cruz (Division chair) and Arthur O. Malabaguio concurring. To understand it, he supplies a backgrounder on plunder (RA 7080, approved July 12, 1991) vs graft (RA 3019, effective August 17, 1960) vs Revised Penal Code crimes (effective 'believe it or not' January 1, 1932); plunder is a relatively new crime. Per Jinggoy Estrada v. Sandiganbayan (February 26, 2002), the anti-plunder law was 'crafted to avoid the mischief and folly of filing multiple informations' in the aftermath of the Marcos regime, where the 'multitude and magnitude' of acts produced a 'legal nightmare' - and the law helped unclog dockets while letting prosecutors aggregate predicate acts (malversation, bribery, RA 3019 violations) into a single plunder charge punishable by reclusion perpetua to death. Here, the Office of the Ombudsman prosecutors charged Napoles separately with 16 RA 3019 violations AND filed a separate plunder charge against Sen. Ramon Revilla Jr. and others (including Napoles) using these very same violations as predicates. Since Revilla et al. were earlier acquitted of plunder for the prosecution's failure to prove the predicate crimes beyond reasonable doubt, Napoles could no longer be found guilty of the same unproven predicate acts. Justice Econg's 'masterpiece' patiently narrated the trial testimonies, especially of Benhur Luy, identical to those in the plunder case - and Panganiban suggests she could have shortened her decision by referring to and not reproducing them. He concurs with the Sandiganbayan - though Napoles remains detained on other pending cases. Regardless of whether he agrees with the prior Revilla acquittal, he is bound by such judgment. The OBM prosecutors committed the 'legal nightmare' of multiple prosecutions that the anti-plunder law sought to avoid - and are 'lucky Justice Econg did not chastise them for committing this legal blunder.' He closes with a tribute: Division chairman Justice Efren N. de la Cruz - known as reliable, credible, honest, competent, IMHO 'should have been promoted to the Supreme Court long ago.' The wish is no longer possible because de la Cruz reaches compulsory retirement next year while the next SC vacancy is in June 2025; three of his former Sandiganbayan colleagues (Teresita J. Leonardo-de Castro, Diosdado M. Peralta, and Alexander G. Gesmundo) were promoted and all became Chief Justices - and de la Cruz preceded CJ Gesmundo in the Sandiganbayan.
